Messed up times By Pastor Jim Hopkins The near consensus of biblical scholars is that though there is a Mark 16: 9-20 these verses were not in the earliest manuscripts of the gospel and were likely added by scribes who found the original ending, Mark 16:8, unsatisfactory because of its emphasis on the fear, confusion and bewilderment of the followers of Jesus who visited his tomb and found it empty. The verse reads — So they went out and fled from the tomb, for terror and amazement had seized them; and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid. One can see why the scribes wanted a happier ending. Yet, the ending original ending is consistent with the way Mark frequently describes the disciples, easily confused and often afraid, understandable in light of an event as shocking as the resurrection and connected to the lives of the hearers and readers of the gospel. We too are often confused, bewildered and afraid. I would argue that Mark ends his gospel the way he does to teach us that our faith is that the love of God meets us in our fear and carries us to God’s new day. We are living in a time in which fear, confusion and bewilderment abound. They seem to be our constant companions. They show up in our waking and in our sleeping. Many of us would describe our world as messed up. Mark would most certainly understand this. He would not, however, want us to be stuck in our fear. He would argue that though fear is real, it need not rule. He would urge us not to let the messed up times we live in mess us up. He would point out that though there are many reasons to be confused and bewildered, we have the resources of our faith to turn to and these resources, the way of Jesus, the community of the church, the promise of resurrection and the hope of God’s new day, sustain and shape us and the communities of faith of which we are a part. In these times I find the prayer I offer to begin my day ever more meaningful. Loving God, Help me to be a blessing to someone today. For my family I pray safety. For my enemies I pray grace. For the world I pray peace. It is my intent to live mindfully and gratefully and to walk in the way of Jesus Amen. Messed up times need not mess us up. articles.text: The following letter was written by community members and read by Susy Struble at the City Council Meeting on Monday, June 16. Editor: We are writing as concerned residents to request further clarification of the City of Piedmont’s policies, practices, contracts and MOUs regarding the sharing of data collected through our 58 Automated License Plate Readers (ALPRs). This surveillance includes images and license plate data for all vehicles entering Piedmont, along with time and location information. This surveillance data can be used to infer the identity, associations, and movement patterns of a car’s occupants. We are deeply alarmed over recent problematic immigration raids in California and in our local area and worry that our local surveillance system is being used to support civil immigration enforcement, potentially in violation of state and federal protections. This is not an unwarranted concern. There are numerous, well documented instances of ICE and other federal agencies accessing surveillance systems – directly and indirectly – to inform immigration raids, many of which are of dubious legality and increasing militarization. Given this context, we believe the City of Piedmont should conduct a thorough review of all ALPR-related governance documents and agreements to ensure compliance with state law and alignment with our community’s values. The goal is to: • Identify any gaps, conflicts or inconsistencies in policies, practices, contracts and MOUs. • Update as needed. Specifically, we recommend the City conduct a review of: • Policy 422 (Immigration Violations) • Policy 438 (Automated License Plate Readers) • The Master Services Agreement (MSA) with Flock Safety • Any related MOUs, including any that have not been publicly shared Some areas to review include, but are not limited to: • Our relationship with the Northern California Regional Intelligence Center (NCRIC, aka “fusion center”). According to the ALPR transparency portal, NCRIC has access to our surveillance data. When residents raised concerns about this a decade ago, Piedmont cited NCRIC’s free surveillance data hosting as a justification. However, Flock now hosts this data. If there is an MOU between NCRIC and the City of Piedmont, do its terms and oversight and enforcement mechanisms align with CA law and our community’s values? • Flock’s data sharing capabilities. These might present a risk of unauthorized access by federal agencies in ways that could violate the California Values Act or our department’s commitment to non-cooperation with civil immigration enforcement. For example, Flock MSA §5.3 states Flock may disclose footage to law enforcement or federal officials if “legally required” or based on “good faith belief” of necessity. This could bypass local oversight and possibly violate CA law. • Oversight gaps with the ALPR transparency portal. Again, it’s unclear if Flock must disclose external queries, such as from a federal agency like ICE or DHS. Moreover, while we appreciate Piedmont’s early adoption of this feature from Flock, the data presented does not help the public understand who has queried our ALPR data, what data is collected and tagged (it’s more than “vehicles, license plates”) and for what purpose in each instance. We applaud Chief Bowers’ thoughtful, consistent leadership and his team’s efforts to ensure their essential work aligns with our community’s values. We also recognize the City must navigate a complex and often ambiguous legal landscape. Still, we believe more should be done to ensure no part of our surveillance infrastructure is used to support civil immigration enforcement in a way that violates state law or community trust. We urge the City to adopt, publish, and actively enforce stronger, clearer policies that prevent misuse of local surveillance data and uphold our community values of the rule of law, civil liberties, and democratic accountability. Thank you for your time, attention and continued transparency on this important issue. With respect and gratitude, Fairuz Abdullah Shanti Brien Irene Cheng David Cole Maya Guzdar Diana Lee Jonah Sachs Susy Struble Liz Tahawi Katy Bradford Vosburg

We urge the City to adopt, publish, and actively enforce stronger, clearer policies that prevent misuse of local surveillance data and uphold our community values of the rule of law, civil liberties, and democratic accountability. articles.text: Piedmont City Council voted unanimously to adopt the proposed budget for FY2025-26 after a second hearing at their regular meeting on Monday, June 16. The budget provisions City funds starting on July 1. The budget, adopted annually, serves as a major policy document and describes how Piedmont intends to finance its services and infrastructure in the coming year. This year’s budget was presented by retired Finance Director Michael Szczech, performing interim duties while the City awaits the arrival of its next appointed Finance Director, Kiran Bawa. The budget, first presented in Council Chambers on June 2, features a General Fund of approximately $40 million. A $8.3 million spending plan for the Facilities Capital Fund was included for work finishing projects to include the community pool and police/fire dispatch center. The adopted budget includes a “modest” change from the first hearing of $10,300. The budget hearing reported a current status with expected revenue $1.2 million above the current year’s budget, with expenditures expected to be lower than budgeted by $1.6 million. With an expected surplus around $3.6 million, City staff recommended that $850,000 of it be transferred from the General Fund to the City’s Equipment fund, keeping the remainder for next year’s budget. The Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee’s written report to Council endorses the proposed plan, stating: “The proposed budget for FY 25-26 reflects the City’s continued commitment to conservative budgeting and financial discipline. This approach ensures that the City can continue to provide high quality public services, replace aging equipment, and address infrastructure repairs, while retaining a strong General Fund.” The Committee’s report encourages the City to further quantify and plan for future infrastructure costs. The Committee also reiterates their call from previous reports for the City to explore options for additional revenue sources, including an increase in the Transfer Tax. Councilmember Tom Ramsey asked at the meeting about how much funding would be needed to bring Piedmont streets up to higher standards, revisiting a previous discussion of paving and road maintenance costs from the previous Council meeting. “That is a question I think we’ll be able to better answer once we develop our new pavement management program, which is something we’ll look to certify by the end of August,” said Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. “...we’re about two to three months away from having those numbers finalized.” Gonzales confirmed that it is likely that additional funds will be required to properly maintain or improve existing road conditions in Piedmont. Gonzales estimated this funding gap to be around $800,000-850,000 per year. The overall budget is meant to embrace priorities presented in a series of City Council Study Sessions, including completion of the community pool, completion of the dispatch center project, the undertaking of the Dearing Memorial Project, and planning for the future public safety building project. articles.text: David Martin’s House Party big band will perform in Piedmont Park on the 4th of July this year immediately following the parade. The concert will begin at approximately 12:00 p.m. on a large stage in the park. One of San Francisco’s premier party bands for 25 years, this interactive 11-piece all-star group has gained a national reputation for their high energy performances, incredible musical variety, and “anything-can-happen” hi-jinx. Past appearances include The Waldorf Astoria in New York City, special Napa Valley performances for Wine Spectator Magazine, concertizing in Maui at the Hyatt Regency Kaanapali and La Costa Resort in Carlsbad; selling out in Reno at the Grand Sierra Resort’s VIP New Years Eve 2010; and entertaining at numerous benefit galas in the greater Bay Area. David Martin is a Bay Area native who began his musical career at the age of six. Known for his powerful vocals and sparkling guitar work, David was a founding member of legendary San Francisco “New Wave” faces The Lloyds and The Buzztones. Martin has assembled a remarkable group of established musician/entertainers including Bobby Strickland (Todd Rundgren, Phil Lesh), Byron Allred (Steve Miller, Todd Rundgren), Gerald Goudeau (Race & Rhythm), Christina Sabatelli (Tubes, Starship), Tim Allen (Silvercreek), Timo Guierrez (Viva Brazil), John Mader (Booker T, Pee Wee Ellis), and Rob Russ (Eddie Money). Rounding out the group’s lineup are the dance artists Sandra Leathley and Stephanie Romano. Dave Martin’s House Party big band will perform in Piedmont on the 4th of July.

articles.text: Piedmont elementary schools will teach English and language arts with a new curriculum next year, Fishtank Learning, a knowledge-based curriculum. The change formally began two years ago and moves away from Lucy Calkins’ “Units of Study” towards a “science of reading” based curriculum. In the May 28 Piedmont School Board meeting the first reading of the action item was conducted and on June 11, the change was approved with a second reading. “Really, this is a paradigm shift for our district,” said Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich. “This committee does not make this recommendation lightly. We recognize the shift that it will entail moving forward, but feel confident with the recommendation.” Dolowich described the report to the board, beginning by summarizing some of the former curricula’s problems. “A few [limitations of Calkins’ system] include a lack of sufficient systematic and explicit instruction in foundational skills such as phonics and fluency, inadequate opportunities to engage in complex and rich texts, and, thirdly, a lack of building background knowledge and vocabulary development for our students,” he said. This past school year, the English Language Arts Adoption Committee, which included nine teachers, evaluated eight alternative curriculum, before narrowing the options down to two, Benchmark and Fishtank, to pilot with students. Twenty-one elementary teachers participated in the piloting of the two new options, of which Fishtank Learning was selected. Wildwood School first grade teacher Amiee Peri spoke for the pilot teachers on May 28. “The main difference is that Benchmark uses short stories, many of which are authored by curriculum writers, and Fishtank uses full length novels that are high quality, rich literature and capture authentic voices of authors of varied cultures and backgrounds,” said Peri. School Board President Lindsay Thomasson explained the process which took two years. “DIBELS was the very first step, and then ‘From Phonics to Reading’ and Spellography adopting those, and then this is the final step in the curriculum adoption process,” said Thomasson. From Phonics to Reading has already been implemented for Piedmont K-3 students. “We’ve seen a lot of success with [From Phonics to Reading] over the last two years. It’s pretty exciting, especially at a first grade level, to see reading and spelling grow for kids,” said Peri. School Board Vice President Ruchi Medhekar spoke in superlatives about the change. “This will be one of the moments that I will remember the most, when I look back at my time on the board,” said Medhekar. Piedmont teachers at all elementary sites will be using Fishtank Learning’s texts and lessons in the fall.

articles.text: First year Piedmont High School Athletic Director Tyler Small provided a report on the recent year of athletics to the school board on June 11. The report included the status of Title IX compliance. Title IX efforts focused on improvement to weight room access, locker room usage, more tournament participation, and more concession sales during home events for girls’ teams with the overarching goal of balancing participation. In total, there were 373 female students at PHS and 413 males. Females account for 47.5% of the student body. When counting two- and three-sport athletes multiple times, there were 365 female athletes and 431 male athletes. Girls sports teams would need to add 24 athletes onto their rosters to achieve equal participation with the boys. To balance participation Small is focusing 2025-26 efforts on increasing participation in girls water polo and swimming when the new community pool opens. The district will also continue to search for local opportunities for beach volleyball practice and competitions. “Traveling to Santa Rosa, or to Santa Cruz or to somewhere on the coast for [beach volleyball] matches, it wears on the athletes, the coaches, the families that are transporting the athletes,” said Small. “The closest competition [girl’s beach volleyball] had was Livermore.” Two strength and conditioning coaches were hired at the start of the year for the weight room, and designated times were allotted for female athletes and middle school athletes. Small said locker room usage was improved by increasing communication around scheduling and by giving more coaches keys to the Witter Field weight room. New to the school, girls’ JV basketball team went to a tournament in Reno, while both girls’ and boys’ golf teams played in invitational tournaments. The varsity girls and boys sports teams each participated in 14 tournaments each. Small highlighted the revitalization of the football program. “Our football program has continued to grow. Hats off to the amazing coaches, who took a program that was almost non-existent and almost cut, due to a lack of interest, and have grown that to over 60 athletes. Next year’s numbers look very similar,” said Small. Small called 2024-25 a “banner year” with four WACC12 Players of the Year and one CIF Norcal Championship in boys soccer. Small also highlighted the 58 first-team WACC12 selections, 54 second-team selections and 35 honorable mention selections. “For a school of 800 students going up against Berkeley, a school of 4000, and going against O’Dowd, a private school, to be able to have those numbers within our league is pretty astounding,” he said. Piedmont’s Title IX compliance was sparked by a gender equity audit of the high school athletic program in 2021-22.
articles.title: Athletics end of year and Title IX report

articles.text: When most people think of a speech therapist, they imagine someone helping a child say their “R” sounds or overcome a lisp. While articulation therapy is one important aspect of the field, it’s only the tip of the iceberg. Speech-language pathologists (SLPs) are trained to assess and treat a broad spectrum of communication and swallowing challenges across the lifespan. Here are ten lesser-known— but equally important—areas where SLPs make a difference: • Language Delays and Disorders SLPs help children who struggle to understand language (receptive) or use language to express themselves (expressive). This includes kids who speak in very short phrases, have trouble following directions, or are late to talk. • Social Communication Individuals with autism, ADHD, or social anxiety may need support learning conversational skills, reading body language, or understand humor and sarcasm. These “hidden rules” of communication are crucial for building friendships. • Feeding and Swallowing Disorders Yes, we help with eating too! Children who choke, gag, or have difficulty transitioning to solids may benefit from feeding therapy. SLPs also work with medically complex infants and children who use feeding tubes. Adults may benefit from swallowing therapy post stroke, head injury or other neurological conditions. • Stuttering and Fluency Fluency disorders like stuttering can cause emotional stress for both children and adults. SLPs provide strategies to improve speech flow, manage tension, and build confidence. • Voice Disorders A hoarse or breathy voice that persists could signal a voice disorder. SLPs work with children who strain their voices, speak too loudly, or have vocal nodules— often caused by yelling or poor vocal habits. • Literacy and Pre-Reading Skills SLPs address phonological awareness, decoding, spelling, and reading comprehension. Many children with language impairments also struggle with reading, and early intervention can change their academic trajectory. • Cognitive Communication After brain injuries or neurological conditions, people may need help with memory, attention, problem-solving, or organizing their thoughts. SLPs help rebuild these skills. • Alternative and Augmentative Communication (AAC) When speaking isn’t possible, SLPs help children and adults communicate through devices, picture boards, or sign language. AAC gives a voice to those who don’t use verbal speech. • Accent Modification and Voice Coaching Some individuals seek help modifying an accent or refining their speaking voice for professional or personal reasons. SLPs offer evidence-based strategies for achieving clear, confident communication. • Selective Mutism and Anxiety-Related Disorders Some children speak comfortably at home but remain silent in school or public. SLPs work collaboratively with psychologists and families to gently increase communication in different settings. Speech therapy is a dynamic and evolving field that touches nearly every aspect of communication—from birth through adulthood. If you or someone you love struggles with speech, language, or swallowing, know that help is available. It’s not just about saying “S” or “R” correctly—it’s about making sure every voice is heard. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of SPEECH Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language, reading and writing. She can be reached at kathryn.pengilly@speechinc. com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com. S P E E C H , I N C .

On the agenda: approval of a new policy on artificial intelligence, one-year contract extensions for top district leaders, review of the Local Control Accountability Plan (LCAP), and adoption of several district budgets. The board is expected to approve next year’s general fund budget. Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD) projects $56,578,194 in revenue for the upcoming school year, with expenditures coming in $618,690 below that total. The district anticipates ending the year with a $4.3 million reserve. Budget forecasts for future years will also be presented. If approved, one-year contract extensions for the superintendent, chief business officer, and assistant superintendent would keep them in their roles through 2028. Contract negotiations with employee unions will not address salaries at this time but will reopen discussions on other areas, including work hours and committee participation. According to board documents, the district wants to revisit topics such as the structure of the professional day, the seven-period schedule, field trips, collaboration time, online training, bell schedules—including the Academy program—as well as union release time and grading timelines. Summer Thoughts Not just articulation: 10 things speech therapists treat By Katie Penguilly When most people think of a speech therapist, they imagine someone helping a child say their “R” sounds or overcome a lisp. While articulation therapy is one important aspect of the field, it’s only the tip of the iceberg. Speech-language pathologists (SLPs) are trained to assess and treat a broad spectrum of communication and swallowing challenges across the lifespan. Here are ten lesser-known— but equally important—areas where SLPs make a difference: • Language Delays and Disorders SLPs help children who struggle to understand language (receptive) or use language to express themselves (expressive). This includes kids who speak in very short phrases, have trouble following directions, or are late to talk. • Social Communication Individuals with autism, ADHD, or social anxiety may need support learning conversational skills, reading body language, or understand humor and sarcasm. These “hidden rules” of communication are crucial for building friendships. • Feeding and Swallowing Disorders Yes, we help with eating too! Children who choke, gag, or have difficulty transitioning to solids may benefit from feeding therapy. SLPs also work with medically complex infants and children who use feeding tubes. Adults may benefit from swallowing therapy post stroke, head injury or other neurological conditions. • Stuttering and Fluency Fluency disorders like stuttering can cause emotional stress for both children and adults. SLPs provide strategies to improve speech flow, manage tension, and build confidence. • Voice Disorders A hoarse or breathy voice that persists could signal a voice disorder. SLPs work with children who strain their voices, speak too loudly, or have vocal nodules— often caused by yelling or poor vocal habits. • Literacy and Pre-Reading Skills SLPs address phonological awareness, decoding, spelling, and reading comprehension. Many children with language impairments also struggle with reading, and early intervention can change their academic trajectory. • Cognitive Communication After brain injuries or neurological conditions, people may need help with memory, attention, problem-solving, or organizing their thoughts. SLPs help rebuild these skills. • Alternative and Augmentative Communication (AAC) When speaking isn’t possible, SLPs help children and adults communicate through devices, picture boards, or sign language. AAC gives a voice to those who don’t use verbal speech. • Accent Modification and Voice Coaching Some individuals seek help modifying an accent or refining their speaking voice for professional or personal reasons. SLPs offer evidence-based strategies for achieving clear, confident communication. • Selective Mutism and Anxiety-Related Disorders Some children speak comfortably at home but remain silent in school or public. SLPs work collaboratively with psychologists and families to gently increase communication in different settings. Speech therapy is a dynamic and evolving field that touches nearly every aspect of communication—from birth through adulthood. If you or someone you love struggles with speech, language, or swallowing, know that help is available. It’s not just about saying “S” or “R” correctly—it’s about making sure every voice is heard. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of SPEECH Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language, reading and writing. Athletics end of year and Title IX report By Jay Russell First year Piedmont High School Athletic Director Tyler Small provided a report on the recent year of athletics to the school board on June 11. The report included the status of Title IX compliance. Title IX efforts focused on improvement to weight room access, locker room usage, more tournament participation, and more concession sales during home events for girls’ teams with the overarching goal of balancing participation. In total, there were 373 female students at PHS and 413 males. Females account for 47.5% of the student body. When counting two- and three-sport athletes multiple times, there were 365 female athletes and 431 male athletes. Girls sports teams would need to add 24 athletes onto their rosters to achieve equal participation with the boys. To balance participation Small is focusing 2025-26 efforts on increasing participation in girls water polo and swimming when the new community pool opens. The district will also continue to search for local opportunities for beach volleyball practice and competitions. “Traveling to Santa Rosa, or to Santa Cruz or to somewhere on the coast for [beach volleyball] matches, it wears on the athletes, the coaches, the families that are transporting the athletes,” said Small. “The closest competition [girl’s beach volleyball] had was Livermore.” Two strength and conditioning coaches were hired at the start of the year for the weight room, and designated times were allotted for female athletes and middle school athletes. Small said locker room usage was improved by increasing communication around scheduling and by giving more coaches keys to the Witter Field weight room. New to the school, girls’ JV basketball team went to a tournament in Reno, while both girls’ and boys’ golf teams played in invitational tournaments. The varsity girls and boys sports teams each participated in 14 tournaments each. Small highlighted the revitalization of the football program. “Our football program has continued to grow. Hats off to the amazing coaches, who took a program that was almost non-existent and almost cut, due to a lack of interest, and have grown that to over 60 athletes. Next year’s numbers look very similar,” said Small. Small called 2024-25 a “banner year” with four WACC12 Players of the Year and one CIF Norcal Championship in boys soccer. Small also highlighted the 58 first-team WACC12 selections, 54 second-team selections and 35 honorable mention selections. “For a school of 800 students going up against Berkeley, a school of 4000, and going against O’Dowd, a private school, to be able to have those numbers within our league is pretty astounding,” he said. Piedmont’s Title IX compliance was sparked by a gender equity audit of the high school athletic program in 2021-22. READ IT IN THE POST

Throughout the summer the Post prints a sampling of letters written by kids attending Camp Augusta, Piedmont’s residential camp at Lake Vera outside Nevada City in the Sierra foothills. Founded in 1931, the camp remains a vital part of the life of hundreds of children each summer. There were more than 75 “Playstation” activities, which are the opposite of the console — whimsical, natural games played with real humans, in real time, with collective creative joy. The new counselors were excitedly nervous for their first campers, even after 25 days and nearly 300 hours of training. The returning staff were excited to see old campers, and greet the new ones. articles.text: Piedmont City Council received an update on the city’s greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and progress on its Climate Action Plan at its regular meeting on Monday, June 16. While the report shows that Piedmont continues to make significant reductions in emissions, it also warns that the city is unlikely to meet its 2030 target without further action. The update follows the city’s 2018 adoption of Climate Action Plan 2.0 (CAP 2.0), which set a goal of reducing emissions 50% from 2005 levels by 2030, and reaching carbon neutrality by 2045. The presentation was delivered by Climate Fellow Andrew Kaplowitz, who authored this year’s GHG inventory. Kaplowitz joined the city through the Sustainability Service Corps Fellowship Program, which had previously supplied climate fellows to Piedmont for nine years. Fellows have played key roles in emissions reporting, public outreach, and development of the city’s REACH building codes. “For nine years, fellows have been vital to advancing the climate action here in Piedmont,” said Planning Director Kevin Jackson. “Fellows have worked on developing the city’s REACH codes, annual greenhouse gas emissions inventories, and have been essential in public engagement.” Kaplowitz’s own fellowship was nearly cut short. On April 26, the federal AmeriCorps program suspended the fellowship as part of broader national budget cuts. The City quickly responded, hiring Kaplowitz as a part-time temporary Sustainability Clerk using unspent Planning Department salary funds to ensure continuity and completion of his work. 2023 Greenhouse Gas Inventory According to the 2023 GHG inventory, Piedmont has reduced its total emissions by 32.1% compared to 2005. Transportation and building energy continue to dominate the city’s emissions profile, accounting for roughly 97% of all emissions. Among transportation sources, passenger vehicles made up 90.5% of the sector’s emissions—representing about 45% of total citywide emissions. In the building energy category, residential natural gas usage made up 92.6%— another 44% of the total. Climate Fellow Andrew Kaplowitz presents the Climate Action Update. Municipal operations, such as the city’s vehicle fleet and employee commutes, made up just 3.5% of Piedmont’s total emissions. However, overall emissions ticked up slightly—by 1.35% from 2022. Kaplowitz attributed the increase largely to a rise in residential natural gas use, as more residents spent time at home due to remote work. Warmer weather and more hot days likely drove higher use of air conditioning as well. These trends, Kaplowitz noted, underscore the urgency of electrification efforts identified in CAP 2.0. Despite the uptick, other emissions categories showed improvement from 2022: • Transportation emissions declined 2.2% • Water and wastewater emissions dropped 41.2%, hitting their lowest levels since 2016 • Electricity-related emissions fell 20.9% Looking Ahead Despite encouraging trends, Piedmont remains off track to meet its 2030 emissions target, according to analysis provided by ICLEI – Local Governments for Sustainability. Kaplowitz’s report emphasized several key strategies for bridging the gap: • Encourage EV adoption and green transportation • Amplify home electrification and energy efficiency • Promote climate-related rebates and public engagement • Incentivize low-carbon commuting options for city staff • Upgrade when and where suitable for efficiency The city also plans to finalize its Electrification Strategy, conduct an energy audit of city facilities, and increase climate-oriented community outreach in the coming year. The Hidden Carbon Footprint The report also noted that the city’s annual inventories do not include lifecycle emissions—the greenhouse gases associated with the production, transportation, and disposal of goods and services consumed outside Piedmont’s borders. If included, emissions would be seven times higher than the current inventory suggests. “If included, Piedmont is the highest emitter per capita in Alameda County due to higher consumption of goods,” the report reads. “While these immense consumption-based emissions pose a significant challenge, they also demonstrate the power Piedmonters yield to curb climate change with their purchasing decisions.” Future Growth as a Climate Variable One major upcoming decision with climate implications is the city’s Moraga Canyon Housing Project, which proposes building up to 199 units on cityowned land. In a June 13 newsletter, local climate advocacy group Piedmont Connect warned that emissions from the housing development could offset most of the gains the city has made over the past decade. The project has not yet been formally evaluated in the city’s climate models, but its potential to increase demand for transportation and energy will likely factor into future CAP updates. As Piedmont plans for a growing population, its climate strategy faces a central challenge: how to accommodate that growth while continuing to drive emissions down. articles.text: On June 14, Jasper and Josie Schuetz strongly represented Piedmont Mountain Bike Team at the Lost and Found Gravel Festival, an annual gravel-bike showcase held in Portola set among the rugged backcountry of the Lost Sierra by the Feather River. The festival features three challenging routes – 40, 64, and 96 miles, each demanding a mix of pavement, dirt, and gravel. Riders traverse scenic ranchlands, high-Sierra valleys, mountain lakes, wildflower meadows, and historic railroad tracks along the Feather River, offering both physical challenge and natural beauty, all at nearly 5,000 feet in elevation. The race and festival is a fundraiser for Sierra Buttes Trail Stewardship, supporting sustainable trail development and the “Connected Communities” network across 15 mountain towns. Jasper Schuetz, 17, co-captain of the Piedmont Mountain Bike Team, has been on a remarkable streak, racking up wins this year. After the regular NICA NorCal Mountain Bike Season ended, he kicked off summer racing on May 30 at the Wente 8-Hour Mountain Bike Race. He teamed up with Sophia Tripovich (Team Schmirk Zone) to claim first place in the Co-Ed 2-Person category, completing 11 laps by beating out pro cyclist Levi Leipheimer and his partner. He followed up that win by taking first place in the Men’s Junior Division (13–18) at Lost and Found, riding the “Full Bull” Jasper Schuetz (middle) atop the podium of the Lost and Found “Full Bull” Course Junior Men’s category. articles.text: Preview of this year’s course and favorite riders This year’s Tour de France marks the 112th edition of La Grande Boucle. Starting with the Grand Départ in Lille on Saturday, July 5, the tour will once again feature its iconic finish along the Champs-Élysées in Paris on July 27. The race concluded last year due to the Olympic Hames underway in Paris. This year’s race will be entirely on French soil, the first time since 2020 that the entirety of the race wo;; ne within France. Lille hosts its first Grand Départ since 1994. Day 1 opens with a 184.9 kilometer flat course around the city. Stage 2 to Boulogne marks the longest stage of the entire tour at 209.1 km on a hilly course, while Stage 3 is a 178.3 km flat course to Dunkirk, while Stage 4 is another hilly course on a 174.2 km ride to Rouen. Stages 5 is one of two individual time trials on a 33 km sprint through Caen. Stages 6-7 provides a collective 398.5 km of hilly riding, while Stages 8-9 are continuous flat courses with 345.5 km collectively. Le Tour turns up in Stage 10 on Bastille Day, July 14, for the first mountain course, 165.3 km from Ennezat to Le Mont Dore with 4,400 meters of climbing. After a rest day, Stage 11 is a 156.8 km ride through the city of Toulouse, which is a precursor to a return to the mountains. Stage 12 is a 181 km ride from Auch to Hautacam with three different steep ascents, including a summit finish. Stage 13 is a unique 10 km time trial on a mountain course that’s completely uphill. Stages 14 is another mountain ride, 182.6 km from Pau to Superbagnères, featuring four steep ascents and a third consecutive summit finish. Stage 15 is another 169.3 km hilly stage followed by their second rest day. They’ll need the rest with three of the next four stages on mountain courses. Stage 16 rides 171.5 km from Montpellier up Mont Ventoux, where the course will have just one huge ascent with a gradient of 8.8 percent to a summit. After a 160.4 km Stage 17, Stages 18-19 provides 301.4 km of mountain riding. Stage 18 has three steep ascents with grades of 5.5 percent, 7.9 percent, and 6.5 percent and a summit finish. Stage 19 also has three steep climbs and another summit finish. Stage 20 is a 185 km hilly course with fluctuating ascents and descents throughout the ride. The finale on July 27’s Stage 21 is a 132.3 km flat ride from Mantes la Ville to Paris. Provided are the five riders to watch based on odds makers. • Tadej Pogačar UAE Team Emirates Slovenia’s Tadej Pogačar is the hands-down favorite after winPhoto courtesy of LeTour.com Map of the 112th Tour de France winding 3,338.8 km through France. ning his third Grand Tour last year and seeking to become the first four-time winner since Chris Froome. He goes to France with a head of steam after winning the Critérium du Dauphiné earlier this month. • Jonas Vingegaard Visma–Lease a Bike Danish rider Jonas Vingegaard won the Yellow Jersey in 2022 and 2023, and finished second in last year’s tour. He is the No. 2 candidate to win this year’s General Classification. • Remco Evenepoel Soudal–Quick-Step A 25-year-old Belgian, Remco Evenepoel, is odds makers’ third favorite after finishing third in last year’s Tour de France. He recently finished fourth in the Critérium du Dauphiné and won the Brabantse Pijl in April. • João Almeida UAE Team Emirates João Almeida is odds makers’ No. 4 favorite, but winning the tour seems less likely given he’s teammates with Pogačar, meaning he’ll likely be a role player in helping push his teammate toward the Yellow Jersey. Helping his cause is several wins this year, including the Tour de Suisse, Tour of the Basque Country, and the Tour de Romandie • Primož Roglič Bora–Hansgrohe Fellow Slovenian Primož Roglič, 35, was leading the 2020 Tour de France entering the second-to-last stage before his countryman Pogačar took the lead in a breathtaking Stage 20 time trial. articles.text: Bear Valley Music Festival begins July 18, marking the 56th anniversary of the eclectic music celebration along Highway 4 that brings together renowned artists and ensembles across genres including classical, jazz, rock, pop and more. The annual summer event is held in the picturesque Bear Valley, nestled in the Sierra Nevada mountains about halfway between Lake Tahoe and Yosemite. Concerts take place under an outdoor tent that seats more than 500 guests. This year’s lineup features everything from ‘80s tribute bands to classic jazz ensembles. “Our main goal as a nonprofit music festival is to build community and create concert events the entire Highway 4 community will enjoy,” said Board of Directors President Julia Mee. “From the Beat to Beethoven, we’ve got something for everyone.” Queen Nation, a Queen tribute band, kicks off the festival Friday, July 18. They are followed Saturday by San Francisco’s Super Diamond, a Neil Diamond tribute band, performing hits from “Sweet Caroline” to “I Am…I Said.” After a week of tribute performances, the festival shifts to classical with Beethoven’s Fifth Symphony on Friday, July 25. The program also features guitarist Lyle Sheffler performing Spanish composer Joaquín Rodrigo’s Concierto de Aranjuez and a work by 18th-century composer Marianna Martines. Soprano singer Carrie Hennessey closes out this year’s festival on August 3. A program featuring music by Mozart and Haydn, interspersed with contemporary pop tunes, takes place Sunday, July 27. The symphonic finale, featuring works by Leonard Bernstein, Erich Wolfgang Korngold and Sergei Rachmaninoff, is scheduled for Friday, Aug. 1. The festival’s annual gala is held Saturday, Aug. 2. Guests are encouraged to wear period attire from the late 19th to early 20th century for an evening of music from the era. Gala tickets include concert admission, a welcome glass of champagne or themed cocktail, dinner with wine, and a live auction. Soprano Carrie Hennessey closes the festival Sunday, Aug. 3. Back by popular demand after last summer’s performance, she will perform fan-favorite songs from Broadway and Hollywood, including music from Les Misérables, The Lion King and The Sound of Music. Visit https://www.bearvalleymusicfestival.org to see the full festival lineup and purchase tickets. Single day tickets are now available. articles.text: Ruth Asawa: Retrospective, the first posthumous retrospective of the groundbreaking work of Californian modernist artist Ruth Asawa, is on display at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) through September. Organized by SFMOMA and New York’s Museum of Modern Art, the exhibition features over 300 works of art including looped-wire hanging sculptures for which Asawa is best known, as well as sculptures, drawings, prints, paintings and archival material from public and private collections. “Ruth Asawa: Retrospective is deeply aligned with SFMOMA’s vision to be both local and global—presenting Bay Area artists with profound significance that also have the potential to be highly impactful and relevant on an international scale,” said Christopher Bedford, Helen and Charles Schwab Director of SFMOMA. “This exhibition provides an opportunity to celebrate the legendary Ruth Asawa, who was both a widely acclaimed artist and a hometown inspiration whose impact can be very much felt today.” Ruth Asawa: Retrospective spans over six decades of the artist’s celebrated career and highlights how her longtime San Francisco home and garden served as a muse for her artwork and informed her public sculpture commissions and dedication to arts advocacy in the city. The posthumous retrospective is co-curated by Janet Bishop, Thomas Weisel Family Chief Curator and Curator of Painting and Sculpture at SFMOMA. “It is an immense privilege to present the full range of Ruth Asawa’s life’s work through this retrospective,” said Bishop. “Not only was Asawa an exceptionally talented artist, among the most distinguished sculptors of the 20th century and a major contributor in so many other mediums, but she lived her values in everything she did, modeling the importance of the arts and opening up creative opportunities for others at every turn.” Ruth Asawa: Retrospective will be on view at SFMOMA through September 2. Visit sfmoma.org or call 415. 357.4000 for more information. Patrons view the Ruth Asawa retrospective at SFMOMA. Photo courtesy of the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art

pages.text: 16 16 Wednesday, June 25, 2025 Arts & Entertainment Bear Valley Music Festival runs July 18 to August 3 By Allyson Aleksey Bear Valley Music Festival begins July 18, marking the 56th anniversary of the eclectic music celebration along Highway 4 that brings together renowned artists and ensembles across genres including classical, jazz, rock, pop and more. The annual summer event is held in the picturesque Bear Valley, nestled in the Sierra Nevada mountains about halfway between Lake Tahoe and Yosemite. Concerts take place under an outdoor tent that seats more than 500 guests. This year’s lineup features everything from ‘80s tribute bands to classic jazz ensembles. “Our main goal as a nonprofit music festival is to build community and create concert events the entire Highway 4 community will enjoy,” said Board of Directors President Julia Mee. “From the Beat to Beethoven, we’ve got something for everyone.” Queen Nation, a Queen tribute band, kicks off the festival Friday, July 18. They are followed Saturday by San Francisco’s Super Diamond, a Neil Diamond tribute band, performing hits from “Sweet Caroline” to “I Am…I Said.” After a week of tribute performances, the festival shifts to classical with Beethoven’s Fifth Symphony on Friday, July 25. The program also features guitarist Lyle Sheffler performing Spanish composer Joaquín Rodrigo’s Concierto de Aranjuez and a work by 18th-century composer Marianna Martines. Soprano singer Carrie Hennessey closes out this year’s festival on August 3. A program featuring music by Mozart and Haydn, interspersed with contemporary pop tunes, takes place Sunday, July 27. The symphonic finale, featuring works by Leonard Bernstein, Erich Wolfgang Korngold and Sergei Rachmaninoff, is scheduled for Friday, Aug. 1. The festival’s annual gala is held Saturday, Aug. 2. Guests are encouraged to wear period attire from the late 19th to early 20th century for an evening of music from the era. Gala tickets include concert admission, a welcome glass of champagne or themed cocktail, dinner with wine, and a live auction. Soprano Carrie Hennessey closes the festival Sunday, Aug. 3. Back by popular demand after last summer’s performance, she will perform fan-favorite songs from Broadway and Hollywood, including music from Les Misérables, The Lion King and The Sound of Music. Visit https://www.bearvalleymusicfestival.org to see the full festival lineup and purchase tickets. Single day tickets are now available. The concert traditionally concludes with a grand finale of spectacular fireworks. SF Symphony performs at Shoreline Amphitheatre July 4 By Allyson Aleksey The San Francisco Symphony will perform its annual Independence Day themed-program on July 4 at Shoreline Amphitheatre, an outdoor venue in Mountain View, playing alongside ukulele virtuoso Taimane. Conductor Edwin Outwater returns to Shoreline Amphitheatre to lead the symphony with a lineup of popular Independence Day classics. The Symphony will be joined by special musical guest Taimane, a Hawaiiborn ukulele virtuoso and songwriter, who makes her Stern Grove debut performing alongside the world-class orchestra on July 6. Taimane is renowned for her unique and inventive style of playing the four-string island instrument and has garnered critical acclaim for her signature stage presence. She is the recipient of the 2023 Nā Hōkū Hanohano Instrumental Album and Instrumental Composition of the Year award, and was recognized as the Nā Hōkū Hanohano Favorite Entertainer of the Year in 2023 and 2019. The concert begins at 8 p.m. and traditionally concludes with a grand finale of spectacular fireworks. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfsymphony.org/ Buy-Tickets/2024-25/SWTSShoreline-4th. articles.text: Oakland artist King Isis will take the stage at the Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) this Friday, June 27, showcasing their unique take on Afrofuturism in music—a blend of R&B, alternative rock, and boho indiepop. King Isis is an emerging pop artist steadily gaining momentum in Oakland’s queer arts scene, known for a fresh, acoustic-forward sound. Their tracks “Dissonance,” “Make it Up,” and “Im fine, thx 4 asking” have garnered hundreds of thousands of views on YouTube. They’ll be joined Friday by DJ Ignacia, whose genre-blending set is designed to get guests dancing. The performance is part of OMCA’s Friday Nights series, a free weekly community event held every Friday at 5 p.m. throughout the spring and summer. The series features live music, hands-on art activities, and late-night museum access with the purchase of a general admission ticket. Guests are encouraged to bring blankets and lawn chairs to relax on the museum’s expansive lawn, where live entertainment continues into the evening. Attendees may bring their own food and nonalcoholic beverages or purchase from on-site food trucks. A rotating selection of vendors will be stationed on 10th Street between Oak and Fallon streets, adjacent to the museum. Outside alcohol is not permitted. Friday Night events are always free and open to the public, but late-night museum access requires a ticket purchase. Visit https://museumca.org/event/friday-nights-at-omca-with-kingisis/ to learn more. King Isis

articles.text: The historic Filoli House and Gardens in Woodside welcomes visitors every Wednesday and Thursday evening throughout the summer for its aptly named “Summer Nights.” Filoli typically closes its grounds at 5 p.m., but on Wednesdays and Thursdays, visitors can explore the historic house and gardens well into the evening. Located 30 miles south of San Francisco and nestled at the foot of the Santa Cruz Mountains, the scenery provides an idyllic backdrop for watching the sun set on a pleasant summer evening. The weekly event features live music by the pool, a pop-up wine and cocktail stand, and a food truck. Some visitors nestle on blankets, while others explore the Estate Trail — a one-mile, self-guided walk through Filoli’s nature preserve. There, it’s not uncommon to spot a family of deer or a gaggle of turkeys along the trail’s five distinct native ecosystems. Filoli’s mission is to “connect [its] rich history with a vibrant future through beauty, nature, and shared stories,” and there is no shortage of natural beauty at the estate. The property is surrounded by more than 23,000 acres of protected Peninsula watershed, and on warm summer evenings, fog can be seen rolling down the mountains. The house was constructed in 1917 and is a notable example of Georgian Revival architecture. Designed by Willis Polk, it took three years to complete and cost $425,000 — roughly $8.5 million in today’s dollars. Built under the direction of William and Agnes Bourn, the estate was originally conceived as a “humble” country home. The Bourn family’s wealth came from gold — specifically the Empire Gold Mine, California’s most productive. “When [the Bourns] built Filoli they were in their 50’s, and were looking to construct a country estate, a common thing for wealthy San Franciscans to do at the time. They chose this spot because of its beautiful location,” explained Susan O’Sullivan, chief external relations officer at Filoli. The Bourns, two of the founding board members of the San Francisco Symphony, loved to entertain. The massive two-story mansion contains 56 rooms, including a ballroom and reception room designed to host concerts and debut balls. The same Baccarat crystal chandeliers from 1917 remain in the ballroom — six-foot-tall glass fixtures that are meticulously cleaned and maintained by Filoli staff. The house spans 54,256 square feet and includes 16 bathrooms, 10 main bedrooms, 14 staff bedrooms and 17 fireplaces. When the Bourns passed away in the 1930s, the house was purchased by William and Lurline Roth, heiress to the Matson Navigation Company. The Roths expanded the gardens to include collections of camellias, rhododendrons and azaleas, and added a swimming pool and screened-in teahouse. Lurline Roth passed away in 1976, and her wish was to donate Filoli so it could be open to the public. In 1977, the estate was given to the National Trust for Historic Preservation. Today, the site is both a California Historical Landmark and listed on the National Register of Historic Places. “Lurline’s wish was that Filoli would be a cultural center for the Bay Area,” O’Sullivan said. “Summer Nights” ends September 18. Learn more about “Summer Nights” at Filoli, and book your visit at https://filoli. org/summer-nights/. Visitors can enjoy live music by the pool during “Summer Nights” events.

articles.text: Former Piedmont resident Bob Houser currently has an exciting exhibit of wood sculptures at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. “I grew up on the edge of a woods in New England and I spent all my free time wandering amongst the trees. Though I have been living in California for all of my adult life, you cannot take the New Englander out of me. It is a part of me. I’m determinedly independent, critically frugal, I don’t take myself too seriously, and yes, there’s the sarcasm. For over 30 years I have been making portraits of people, real people, as a photographer for advertising and editorial clients worldwide. Along the way, I have pictured large sculptural pieces in my mind – pieces I never had the space to create. “Fast forward a few decades of city life, and I’m back living on a farm, this time in the Oakland hills. When I started to make sculpture under the shade of a 60-year-old Cedar, I was back home again, back in the woods of New England, back playing with trees.” Robert Houser

articles.text: 2nd show added at 5:30 p.m. on Saturday, July 12 Derek Gripper is a South African classical guitarist and composer renowned for his unique ability to transcribe and perform complex West African kora music on the classical guitar. His work bridges the gap between different musical traditions and has garnered international recognition for its innovation and virtuosity. Gripper’s journey began with the challenge of how to bring the intricate, flowing music of West Africa’s griots — traditionally played on the 21-string kora — on the guitar? His album One Night on Earth was the answer, a recording so unexpected that celebrated guitarist John Williams said, “It seemed absolutely impossible until I heard Derek Gripper do it.” But this project wasn’t just about technical mastery. It was about creating connection — between African oral traditions and Western classical music, between different ways of listening and understanding. Along the way, Gripper has performed with legendary musicians John Williams and Toumani Diabaté’s Symmetric Orchestra, sharing stages from Carnegie Hall to Shakespeare’s Globe. In his concerts he weaves together the works of composers like Toumani Diabaté, Ali Farka Touré, J.S. Bach, and Arvo Pärt, creating a dialogue where different musical traditions meet. His adventurous spirit and artistry have been recognized by Songlines Magazine more than once: his 2016 album Libraries on Fire was named Best Album in Africa & the Middle East, and his 2024 collaboration with kora master Ballaké Sissoko won Songlines’ Best Album award for that year. Recent projects like A Year of Swimming and his ongoing work with Sissoko blend original compositions, improvisations, and West African and European musical lineages. His recordings of Bach’s solo works reveal surprising links between classical music and the improvisational spirit of the griots. Book your tickets now and be part of the conversation. And speaking of country flair, Leapin’ Louie delivered cowboy comedy with style and skill. Equal parts clever and athletic, he wowed the crowd with rope tricks and slapstick. I spoke to him after his set—turns out he’s performed in 35 countries. The miniature railroad museum was like something out of The Twilight Zone—an odd, mesmerizing little world in motion. On a more humorous note, one small restaurant served an entire menu built around Spam. Oddly enough, Monty Python was nowhere to be found. Spam aside, a friend of mine grilled up a surprisingly good steak. His method broke with tradition: make a marinade with salt and brown sugar (pepper optional), rub it onto the meat, seal it in a plastic bag, and cook it like a regular steak. The result? articles.text: Excitement was everywhere— that’s just how it is when the circus comes to town. PT Barnum, Bailey, and the Ringling Brothers may be long gone, but their spirit was alive and well at the Alameda County Fair. Families crowded the grounds, creating a true cross-section of America. It felt like a fairground collided with a three-ring circus. First, you pay to park, then there’s a nominal admission fee— and then it’s off to the races, so to speak. There was something for everyone. Naturally, we started with food. One of the first stands we passed offered giant turkey legs, billed as “Texas-sized,” for nearly $23. We paired that with a heaping pile of French fries. Everything was oversized. You’d think PT Barnum himself was still running the show. Among the attractions was a breathtaking trapeze act, and the motorcycle acrobatics show was downright heart-stopping. “Terrifying” might be more accurate. The only downside was the announcer’s nonstop shouting of “Let’s make some noise!”— repeated ad nauseam. The piglet races were a surprise hit—those little guys can really move. The announcer laced his commentary with puns and wordplay that kept the crowd The Alameda County Fair is running now through July 6 at the Alameda County Fairgrounds in Pleasanton.
articles.title: Critic’s Day Off

Eager to begin, he initially struggles to find the right angle. Then it dawns on him—the angle is the experience itself. articles.text: What Peter Jackson achieves in They Shall Not Grow Old is extraordinary—bordering on magical. Given access to hundreds of hours of archival footage from Britain’s Imperial War Museum, he set out to make a 30-minute short. The project instead became a years-long restoration feat that transforms how we see World War I. Using cutting-edge technology, Jackson and his team meticulously cleaned and restored the original film—most of it handcranked, shot at varying speeds. They stabilized it to modern 24-frames-per-second, then undertook the painstaking work of colorizing the black-and-white footage. They traveled to original battlefield sites to capture reference photos, ensuring accuracy in landscapes, uniforms, and detail. Lip-readers deciphered what soldiers were saying, and voice actors from the same regions recreated their speech, dialects intact. No narration was added; instead, the film uses excerpts from more than 600 hours of BBC interviews with WWI veterans—100 voices telling their own story. The result feels almost surreal, as if time has folded and we are seeing 1914 through the eyes of those who lived it. The story unfolds chronologically. In the beginning, we see black-and-white footage of young enlistees—some as young as 14 or 15—arriving at boot camp, wide-eyed and eager. The voiceovers reflect a mix of excitement and national pride. Many believed they were embarking on a grand adventure that would be over by Christmas. Britain buzzed with war fever. Men not in uniform were shamed on the streets and handed white feathers—symbols of cowardice—by young women. Posters urged them to enlist and “do their part.” Then, abruptly, the screen shifts to color. The transformation is stunning. They headed behind the Exedra, entered the park’s upper trail, and followed the lower path along Bushy Dell Creek. Towering eucalyptus trees, nourished by the creek for decades, shaded their way. The group paused to read park history trail markers about the Sulphur Springs Grotto, the Eucalyptus Amphitheater, and “the Cascade,” a lush tropical landscape created by Frank C. Havens in the early 1900s. They reached the new bridge, crossed it, and took a group photo. Later, walker Mark Davis researched the creek’s name, which came from the “rural and romantic” character of its surrounding ravine, once called Bushy Dell. Coat the shrimp with lemon juice and 2 tablespoons olive oil, then toss with 2 teaspoons of the spice mix. Set aside in the refrigerator for not longer than 15 minutes. Heat a heavy skillet over medium high heat. Coat with about 1 tablespoon of olive oil. Sear the pork first and cook for about 4 minutes per side. Transfer to a plate and keep warm. In the same pan, add a bit more olive oil if needed, and sear the shrimp; about 2 minutes per side. TO SERVE: Spread some Romesco sauce on a plate, then place the pork and shrimp on top. Drizzle a bit more sauce and olive oil over the top, if desired. Garnish with plenty of chopped parsley. Enjoy! Quick Romesco Sauce Adapted from Chow – Kate Ramos Makes: About 1½ cups • • • • • • • • • INGREDIENTS 1 medium tomato, halved 2 medium garlic cloves, peeled 1 slice crusty bread (about 1 ounce) ¼ cup whole raw almonds 2 red bell peppers 2 tablespoons Sherry vinegar ¼ cup olive oil ½ teaspoon sea salt ½ teaspoon paprika INSTRUCTIONS Place oven rack on middle rung. Preheat the oven to 450°F. Arrange the peppers, tomato (cut side up), garlic, bread and almonds on a rimmed baking sheet and roast until the bread and almonds are lightly toasted, about 5 to 7 minutes. Remove the bread and almonds and set aside. Return the peppers, tomato and garlic to the oven and roast an additional 10–12 minutes; until softened and some browning occurs. Transfer the roasted ingredients to a food processor or blender and pulse to coarsely chop. Add vinegar, olive oil, salt, and paprika and pulse again until well combined and relatively smooth. NOTES: Reserve any remaining spice mix and Romesco sauce for future use. The spice mix may be used on any meats, vegetables, rice and potatoes. Romesco is a classic dipping sauce for vegetables. Trenches are flooded, littered with corpses, and filled with the stench of decay. Blackened arms protrude from the walls of earth. The soldiers spend sleepless nights in dugouts, while the ground shakes from relentless shelling. When the order comes to go “over the top,” they climb out of the trenches and into machinegun fire. Casualties are immense. Those who survive suffer disfigurement, trauma, and loss. Some stare directly into the camera with brittle smiles—already aware of what awaits them. WWI lasted from 1914 to 1918 and was once called “The War to End All Wars.” After watching They Shall Not Grow Old, it becomes painfully clear why people believed it had to be. The scale of devastation is staggering: 5.5 million military dead, 12 million wounded, and more than 4 million civilian casualties. Poison gas alone caused 1.3 million injuries. One million British soldiers—boys, many of them—never returned. For a small island nation, the loss was overwhelming. Yet Jackson offers no commentary—no on-screen text, no judgment. She is incandescent as Starr, and it’s a portrayal in which she inhabits a bright, vital girl who is carefully navigating a journey that soon becomes both harrowing and life altering. Tillman is unflinching, refusing to pull back from revelations large and small that America has yet to overcome the painful realities of racism and socioeconomic inequality. He also acknowledges that life for many Americans, especially those of color, is replete with grays. In a friend way, Starr’s life is an awkward but delineated metaphor that captures this perpetual, sometimes surreal dilemma, meaning that the prisms through which most of us peer are prone to an inherent distortion. To Tillman’s credit he rarely lapses into polemics; rather, he relies in The Hate U Give on point of view from the inside out. There is one tragic moment when Starr bears witness to the death of her childhood friend, Khalil (Algee Smith). Drivshort ing Starr home from a party, he is stopped (something that we immediately know will not end well) and then is devastatingly shot by a white police officer. As the singular witness, Starr is forced to make a moral choice regarding stepping forward or remaining silent. For her it is a nexus of the rock and the hard place and she is tormented by indecision. Her mother (Regina Hall) counsels retreat. Her father, Maverick Carter (an outstanding Russell Hornsby), insists she speak her truth. It’s at this point in the film that a myriad of issues are crystalized as Starr faces questions of identity and morality that up to this point have never intruded into her young life. There is a backstory scene that takes place not long after the film begins. It’s one where her father sits his young children down at the dining room table (Starr is 10, her brother 9), and gives them “the talk,” one that consists of what to do and how to behave if stopped by a white police officer. articles.text: Several crosswalks on Grand Avenue have re-opened for pedestrian traffic, as construction crews wrapped up another phase of the Grand Avenue Repavement Project last week. New concrete bulb-outs— designed to shorten crossing distances and improve safety—were completed at the intersections of Grand and Greenbank and Grand and Linda. The first concrete pours took place Saturday, June 14, with crews finishing the final ramp on Monday, June 16. Temporary asphalt was laid later in the week, allowing the city to reopen the crosswalks. Though back in use, the crossings still require finishing touches before the full project wraps. Final improvements—including new flashing beacons and fresh pavement along Piedmont’s stretch of Grand—are expected by the end of August. “The completion of the bulbouts is an important milestone on the Grand Avenue Pedestrian Safety Project,” said Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. “The contractor’s activities are now shifting to the Grand/Fairview intersection, where they will relocate a sewer pipeline and install new storm drainage pipelines that will service the newly installed green infrastructure facilities. This will take approximately five weeks to complete. We remain on schedule to complete the paving and striping of Grand Avenue by the end of August.” The project will move next to the Grand and Fairview intersection, where crews will begin work on Piedmont’s first bioswale—a vegetated channel designed to naturally filter stormwater. Partial road closures will be in place while this work is underway. New concrete bulb-outs were poured last week, on the corner of Grand and Greenbank Avenues. Concrete work added new features to the sidewalks along Grand Avenue last week. My experience in two Southern states, where they really have a lot of rain, is seeing many projects with crews spreading roofing type membranes over sites much larger than our pool to protect the soil and employing pumps to drain the collected water. Was that type of mitigation discussed here? If there is a claim for this for an extension or for additional services or for the underground issues noted above (Dec.2, 2024 report), I would hope that there would be pushback from the City and the same for all claims where we ask the question; Were alternatives sought which could have mitigated the delay or additional cost? Why do I Care? I opposed the pool project in 2020 because I and others felt that the upgrade of the Essential Services Buildings (ESB) should have the highest priority because of their basic function and that they serve all Piedmont residents not just a segment. I still hold that view, but the pool project is the reality, and I do, of course, want the project to be successful. The project has staggered around a bit from the first bid process to finally finding a low bidder who met the City’s budget estimate. I’ve been critical to the Council of the City’s iterative design process rather than a more controlled model (see piedmontcivic.org – opinion) because of the time lost and the additional fees incurred by design process to date. I want to see an efficient fair project management process – even if only in parts. The ESB project is right ahead of us and will probably triple the cost of the pool. Managing that process and budget in an efficient and prudent way will be paramount. What do I hope will happen? As the pool project appears to wobble along toward some future opening date, I hope the City Council and Staff will be a strong, demanding and fair Owner/Client when the design construction team comes before them on July7th. And that they require more frequent updates. (I say wobble because if you visit the site you will see a jobsite that doesn’t resemble any 90% complete jobsite I have ever been involved in. On Friday, June 20, there were four earth moving vehicles, one major excavation still open, several walls and steps ready for a concrete pour, incomplete cladding on the building exterior. When I dropped by about 2:30 p.m. that afternoon, the site was totally buttoned up. What’s the rush?). I fear that the low bidder served the City well financially at the start of the project but that we may now be paying for that decision with the lackluster performance by the construction team to forecast and meet critical dates which are so important for the City to manage its role in opening the pool. And one personal comment. The Piedmont Post article mentioned “one factor contributing to the recent delays is the unexpected death of project executive George Sanen of Griffin Structures.” That remark is beyond the pale, and I would hope whoever is the source of that comment would retract it and sincerely apologize to Mr. Sanen’s family for it. Sincerely, Donald Chandler, AIA
